mthfr: CDC: MTHFR Gene Variant and Folic Acid Facts
Common-variant and prevention guidance; not personal genetic advice

sections.what: Generic folate names the vitamin family, not a verified chemical preparation.
sections.body: Folate participates in DNA and RNA synthesis, cell division and amino-acid metabolism, including homocysteine-to-methionine reactions. Those normal functions do not establish a benefit from adding more when intake is already adequate.
sections.form: Do not infer folic acid, 5-MTHF, a salt, source or manufacturing process from a generic folate label.
sections.research: A family-level physiological explanation is available, but form-specific findings cannot be assigned until the preparation is named.
sections.high: Large folate intakes can correct the anemia of B12 deficiency without correcting its neurological injury, potentially delaying recognition. Cancer findings depend on timing, population, baseline status and co-interventions; they do not establish a universal ingredient-level cancer verdict.
sections.reference: The US adult upper limit at age 19 and older is 1,000 mcg/day folic acid from supplements and fortified foods, excluding naturally occurring food folate. This folic-acid mass must not be compared directly with mcg DFE or automatically applied to an unverified 5-MTHF preparation. It is not a supplement target. No product conversion or total-intake calculation is performed.
sections.debate: NIH describes inconclusive comparative-benefit research in people with the common MTHFR 677C>T variant and notes that some might benefit from 5-MTHF. CDC states that common variants do not prevent folic-acid processing and are not a reason to avoid it. Folate-status or homocysteine results and prevention of neural tube defects are different outcomes; folic-acid prevention evidence must not be transferred automatically to every folate preparation. These statements do not diagnose a variant or choose a personal regimen.

sections.what: Folic acid is the fully oxidized monoglutamate form of folate used in fortified foods and many supplements.

sections.what: 5-MTHF is a methylated folate form and the main folate form in plasma.
sections.body: Folate participates in DNA and RNA synthesis, cell division and amino-acid metabolism, including homocysteine-to-methionine reactions. Those normal functions do not establish a benefit from adding more when intake is already adequate.

sections.research: Some people with MTHFR 677C>T might benefit, but comparative-benefit research is inconclusive. Biomarker improvements are not proof that 5-MTHF has identical neural-tube-defect prevention evidence or that everyone with a common variant needs it.

sections.what: Generic B12 or cobalamin does not identify the preparation.
sections.body: Vitamin B12 supports normal nervous-system development and function, healthy red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis. It participates in methionine synthesis and methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism. Physiological necessity does not establish an energy or performance benefit from extra B12 when status is sufficient.
sections.form: Do not infer methylcobalamin, cyanocobalamin, adenosylcobalamin or hydroxocobalamin from the generic vitamin name.
sections.research: Deficiency-correction findings are not proof of additional benefit in an adequately nourished person. The name alone does not establish a deficiency or a treatment route.
sections.high: The US Food and Nutrition Board has not established a B12 upper limit because of its low toxicity potential. This is not proof of unlimited benefit or suitability for every person. Mixed observational high-B12/cancer associations do not by themselves prove that supplementation caused cancer.
sections.reference: No US tolerable upper intake level is established for B12. Absence of a limit is not a dose target. Amount, absorption barriers, deficiency severity and route of administration are separate questions; a compound name alone supplies none of those measurements. No treatment dose or intake total is calculated.
sections.debate: NIH reports no evidence that supplement absorption rates differ by B12 form. This is not proof that all routes, doses, formulations and clinical situations are identical. Active-form labels do not establish universal superiority. Sublingual and oral preparations have not shown a general efficacy difference in the studies NIH summarizes, while prescribed injections address different clinical contexts.

records.title: Adenosylcobalamin
records.form_classification: adenosyl; metabolically active B12 form, not methylcobalamin

sections.what: Adenosylcobalamin, also called 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin, is another metabolically active B12 form.

sections.form: It must remain distinct from methylcobalamin. Metabolically active does not mean methylated, and the name does not establish superior clinical benefit.
sections.research: Adenosylcobalamin’s normal coenzyme role does not prove a special energy or exercise benefit from supplementation. Comparative form absorption evidence does not establish a universal best B12 form.

records.title: Hydroxocobalamin / hydroxycobalamin
records.form_classification: converted to active B12 forms; not methylcobalamin

sections.what: Hydroxocobalamin, also called hydroxycobalamin, can be converted to active B12 forms.
sections.body: Vitamin B12 supports normal nervous-system development and function, healthy red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis. sections.form: The body’s conversion of this compound is not evidence that it is ineffective. Oral supplement labels do not establish prescribed injection use or an equivalent absorbed dose.
sections.research: NIH describes prescription parenteral hydroxycobalamin in deficiency care. Route-specific treatment evidence should not become a self-treatment instruction or a benefit claim for an oral product.
